name: Dark Sulphate Green
lede: Dark Sulphate Green is a muted, bluish-leaning green, Robert Ridgway's darker step down from his own Sulphate Green, a chemical-sounding name whose exact sulphate is never named.

sections.title: A chemical's name, darkened
sections.body: Ridgway placed Dark Sulphate Green on plate XIX in 1912, directly below the lighter [[sulphate-green|Sulphate Green]] on the same hue column [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary filed the exact darker name again in 1955, block 164, as a moderate bluish green [2]. Neither source explains which sulphate the family name points to; copperas, a sulphate salt long used in dye vats, is one candidate the books raise for the lighter color, but the link is not documented for either [3]. Its nearest named neighbors on file are [[mint-turquoise]] and [[illuminating-emerald]], both close at 3.4 to 3.6 CIEDE2000 units [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this green, as photographed, in 30 of 23,781 paintings, 0.13 percent, rarer than 66 percent of the named colors we track [5]. It peaks in the 1900s, 6 of 1,674 paintings from that century, 4.4 times the expected rate [5]. The earliest dated match is a Hans Memling painting from 1480, 432 years before Ridgway's plate; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a first [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 42 percent of its 12 strongest matches [5].

origin.named_after: the base color Sulphate Green, darkened; the exact sulphate meant is not documented
